title: Meta-Learning for Robust Robot Control
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-learning to develop robust and adaptable robot control systems. Traditional robot control methods often struggle to generalize to unseen environments, requiring extensive retraining for each new scenario. We propose a framework leveraging meta-learning, where a robot learns to learn control policies through experience across a diverse set of simulated environments. This approach allows the robot to rapidly adapt to novel environments by effectively transferring knowledge gained during prior exploration and learning. The core mechanism relies on accumulating experience through exploration and utilizing meta-learning algorithms to effectively generalize control strategies. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to significantly improve a robot's ability to perform tasks in unfamiliar conditions, addressing a critical challenge in robotics. The proposed system offers a pathway towards more autonomous and adaptable robots capable of operating in dynamically changing environments.

title: Geometric Proof of Computational Complexity for Neural Networks
abstract: The computational complexity of neural networks is a significant challenge in the field of machine learning. Traditional approaches often rely on asymptotic analysis, which can be inadequate for capturing the true complexity. This paper proposes a novel methodology for rigorously proving the computational complexity of neural network training using geometric techniques. We develop a new framework that leverages geometric properties to establish a tighter bound on the runtime required to train a given network. The core mechanism involves representing the neural network's function as a geometric object and applying geometric theorems to derive a computational complexity lower bound. This approach aims to provide a more precise and reliable understanding of the problem, ultimately contributing to the development of more efficient and scalable neural network architectures.

title: Adaptive Topological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network design centered around adaptive topology. The core claim is that the topological structure of a neural network can and should be dynamically adjusted during runtime, contingent upon the learning task and the characteristics of the data. Traditional neural networks operate with a fixed topology, often leading to inefficiencies and suboptimal performance. We introduce Adaptive Topological Neural Networks (ATNNs) which employ a dynamic architecture where nodes can form and break connections, guided by a core mechanism of reinforcement learning or genetic algorithms. The network's topology is optimized based on real-time metrics such as gradient information, information propagation, and computational cost. This allows for a more flexible and efficient learning process, ultimately leading to improved performance and potentially faster convergence. This work represents a significant departure from static network architectures and paves the way for more adaptable and powerful neural network designs. The proposed system is designed to address limitations inherent in fixed topologies, offering a pathway to greater computational efficacy and improved learning outcomes.

title: Microscopic Quantum Field Theory Computational Model
abstract: This paper presents a novel computational model based on the principles of microscopic quantum field theory, designed to simulate the self-organization of quantum systems and enhance quantum information processing. The core mechanism leverages the inherent self-organizing properties of quantum field theories, coupled with quantum entanglement and superposition, to mimic complex quantum behavior and achieve improved efficiency in data manipulation. The model aims to provide a robust and scalable framework for simulating and processing quantum information.

title: Preregistration (Stage 1a): Threshold governance for a white-box/black-box annotation evaluation pipeline
abstract: Stage 1a preregistration for a study on the auditability of LLM-based annotation. This record freezes the form of threshold governance—how decision criteria are to be estimated and updated, the stopping rule, the permitted magnitude of a single update, and the versioning rules—before any annotation data are collected. Numerical values are deliberately deferred to Stage 1b, which will be released as a new version of this record. Files are under embargo until 2026-12-31 to avoid disclosing operational details ahead of the associated manuscript submission. The archive is self-contained: it includes a signed git tag object, a per-file SHA-256 manifest, the signing public key, and a full snapshot of the project's architecture decision records, so that a third party can verify offline that the frozen content has not been altered.

title: FodaOS Unified Field Theory Series V: The Residueon Compiler — Bootstrap Fixed Points, the Residueon-Table Intermediate Representation, and Domain-Order Type Inference
abstract: This paper gives the compiler-theoretic culmination of the FodaOS framework: it turns the five-operator computation of [Paper2] and the residueon-tower mathematics of [Paper4] into an algebraic compiler that is self-bootstrapping, verifiable, and capable of homogeneous multi-backend emission. The core results are organized in seven layers. (i) Intermediate-representation layer — the residueon table (z,r,n)(z,r,n) as the single universal IR; the Kleene bijection theorem (Theorem V1) turns compiler correctness from a test-coverage problem into a machine-decidable fixed-point problem. (ii) Bootstrap layer — the rigorous definition of self-bootstrapping (three constraints + bit-identical) and the three-tier theory (object level C⋅C=CC⋅C=C, meta level Ψ(2)Ψ(2), evolution level), with a capping theorem ruling out a fourth order; this version adds Theorem V36 (Banach contractive bootstrap): the measured Lipschitz constant of the bootstrap iteration is L=poles/tokens∈[0.821,0.878]<1L=poles/tokens∈[0.821,0.878]<1, upgrading the bootstrap fixed point from pigeonhole existence (Theorem V3) to existence, uniqueness, and exponential convergence (fixed-point exponent α=0.234α=0.234 bit/iteration). (iii) Trust layer — the three-compiler triangular cross-check against Thompson's "Reflections on Trusting Trust" attack, plus the fourth-corner cross-language reader. (iv) Pipeline layer — the field-theoretic reconstruction of the four compilation stages (lexical/syntactic/semantic/code-generation) and the layer-collapse theorem, adding Proposition V38 (priority-chain duality group): the seven-level precedence parsing chain carries a (Z/2Z)3(Z/2Z)3 duality structure (logic/comparison/arithmetic, three mutually independent De Morgan–style flips). (v) Type layer — Domain-Order Inference (DOI): seven rules perform constraint solving over the divisibility lattice (composition takes lcmlcm rather than unification; minimization takes the least fixed point), turning the lazy field-extension mathematics of [Paper4] Theorems 23/24 into a compile-time algorithm; shell polymorphism \forall k.\̲t̲a̲u̲@̲k̲ is a new programming-language concept; the five-layer stepless tower (§14.6) automates domain selection into two-coordinate lookup plus lazy pool extension. (vi) Optimization layer — the Möbius conformal view of compilation (optimization passes preserve the cross-ratio invariant) and gear-shift geometry, adding Proposition V37 (structural termination of finite-field equality saturation): the external-fuel dependence of equality saturation (the egg/ROVER/eqsat family) is replaced by the boundedness of the finite-field value space, and an information-theoretic Shannon upper bound is given for residual simplification (measured simplification rate 23.9% versus a source-coding bound of 23.6%); the optimization-pass spectrum (§16.5) is implemented in pure ΨLang in layers. (vii) Physics layer — the homogeneous multi-backend theorem and "the residueon table is the chip mask", adding Proposition V39 (prime-pool–RNS structural correspondence): the prime pool and the modulus chain of RNS-CKKS homomorphic encryption are structurally isomorphic on the NTT-friendly prime admission criterion, together with the industrial-anchor check that 2025 photonic processors (Lightmatter/Lightelligence) have entered production AI workloads. Beneath the axiom layer, this paper introduces a number-theoretic constant layer (§2.4): every compile-time constant must carry an independently re-computable number-theoretic identity (Weyl group order / factorial unification, Coxeter-number arithmetic, Ramanujan–Nagell constants, the 6h+16h+1 prime family), and pushes the conformal view of compilation (Proposition V8) to its first machine-verified finite-group anchor D4=⟨C,I⟩D4=⟨C,I⟩ (generated by the Cayley transform and inversion, elliptic criterion tr2/det⁡=2tr2/det=2, §15.4). All measurements are anchored by the dual-engine bit-identity criterion of the on-machine self-compilation tower (V11-043 through V11-048). This version simultaneously performs thematic convergence: seven results incongruent with the compiler main line (perfect-number image spectra, cognitive-matter phase transitions, vortex–residueon isomorphism, Paley geometric fingerprints, etc.) are removed after review, keeping the main text focused on compiler theory proper. The related-work comparison is extended to seven groups — CakeML (proof-producing bootstrap), the GNU Mes full-source bootstrap chain, the equality-saturation family, RNS homomorphic compilation, ZX-calculus, reversible programming languages, and photonic compilers (§23.8–§23.14).

title: Flux noise without flux tunability in superconducting qubits
abstract: Flux noise is unanimously recognised as a leading dephasing mechanism for flux-tunable superconducting qubits. However, our microscopic understanding remains incomplete, and basic effects like Faraday's law of induction have only very recently come into focus. Based on a quantum geometric description of the Faraday effect, we provide an in-depth derivation of the coupling of generic magnetic sources to thin film superconducting structures, under appropriate consideration of the device geometry. We apply the resulting framework to time-varying magnetic dipoles, describing surface or substrate spins, as well as current-carrying flux lines. We show that flux noise not only affects dephasing, but also provides a fundamental limit for the qubit quality factor - notably, even when the qubit contains no loops and is thus nominally not flux-tunable. Assuming surface spins as the origin for universal flux noise, we expect that this quality factor limit might be reached in the near term. For flux lines, we formulate a minimal safety distance to conserve the qubit performance, potentially constraining the scale-up of quantum hardware. This distance is boosted in the presence of large capacitor wings typical for transmons, due to a lensing of the electromotive field which is largely independent of Meissner screening.

title: Benchmarking RAW and RGB Restoration in Image Signal Processors
abstract: Modern cameras transform RAW sensor measurements into sRGB images through an image signal processor (ISP). We benchmark two placements for blind restoration around a fixed ISP: (A) pre-ISP restoration in the RAW domain and (B) post-ISP restoration in the sRGB domain. The benchmark covers four smartphone device groups, two learned ISPs, three degradation regimes--noise, blur, and joint noise and blur--, and several representative RAW and RGB restoration models. Our results show that placement alone does not determine performance. The RAW restoration strategy outperforms the best generic RGB restoration models. However, RGB restoration models trained considering the ISP transformations, achieve the best overall performance. Our novel benchmark demonstrates that the image reconstruction performance strongly depends on the alignment between the restoration model and the target imaging pipeline. We consequently recommend reporting restoration placement and ISP-aware supervision as key experimental factors. Our code is available at https://github.com/mv-lab/AISP

title: KSG-Net: Key-Sparse and Global-Context Learning for Maritime 3D Ship Detection
abstract: Accurate 3D ship detection in maritime environments is critical for autonomous navigation, yet remains challenging due to large-scale vessel variations, sparse point clouds of small vessels, and severe sea-clutter interference. Existing methods, primarily based on 2D features or dense representations, struggle to balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, while sparse 3D detectors designed for road scenes generalize poorly to maritime scenarios. This paper focuses on two key challenges in maritime LiDAR perception: weak feature representation for small and sparse vessels, and insufficient global structural modeling for large vessels due to the limited receptive field of local sparse convolutions. To address these issues, we propose KSG-Net, a Key-Sparse and Global-Context learning network for maritime 3D ship detection. The core idea is to jointly enhance local discriminative features and global structural awareness within a unified fully sparse detection framework. Specifically, a Key Sparse Multi-scale Aggregation (KSMA) module is designed to enhance the representation of small and sparse vessels by selecting informative key voxels and aggregating cross-scale neighborhood features. Furthermore, a Global Context Aggregation (GCA) module is introduced to capture long-range geometric dependencies through scene-level context modeling with gated residual interactions, thereby improving the representation of large vessels. Extensive experiments on the Thames River vessel dataset and simulated datasets demonstrate that KSG-Net consistently outperforms existing methods in multi-scale vessel detection and exhibits strong robustness in complex maritime environments.

title: L’adoption de l’intelligence artificielle générative au sein des organismes à but non lucratif communautaires du Québec - Conditions facilitantes et freins à l’adoption organisationnelle
abstract: Depuis plusieurs années, l'Obvia accompagne des OBNL, notamment du milieu communautaire québécois, dans leur compréhension des enjeux sociétaux de l'intelligence artificielle. Au fil de ces collaborations, une réalité s'est imposée : les préoccupations de ces organismes ne portent pas seulement sur les impacts de l'IA sur leurs domaines ou leurs populations desservies, mais aussi sur leur propre capacité à s'en saisir. C'est cette observation, formulée par plusieurs partenaires du milieu, qui est à l'origine de cette recherche. Pour la première fois dans le contexte québécois, ce rapport documente, les conditions dans lesquelles les organismes à but non lucratif (OBNL) adoptent, ou non, l'intelligence artificielle générative (IAg). Il examine ces conditions à travers quatre dimensions : les caractéristiques technologiques des outils, les réalités organisationnelles internes, les pressions et ressources de l'environnement externe, et le rôle central des individus dans le processus d'adoption. Ce rapport est l’adaptation d’un projet supervisé d'intervention réalisé par Christophe Kermoison dans le cadre de la maîtrise en Développement organisationnel de HEC Montréal, sous la direction du professeur Gregory Vial, membre chercheur de l’Obvia, et avec l'appui d’un comité aviseur de l'Obvia.

evidence.title: L’adoption de l’intelligence artificielle générative au sein des organismes à but non lucratif communautaires du Québec - Conditions facilitantes et freins à l’adoption organisationnelle
evidence.abstract: Depuis plusieurs années, l'Obvia accompagne des OBNL, notamment du milieu communautaire québécois, dans leur compréhension des enjeux sociétaux de l'intelligence artificielle. Au fil de ces collaborations, une réalité s'est imposée : les préoccupations de ces organismes ne portent pas seulement sur les impacts de l'IA sur leurs domaines ou leurs populations desservies, mais aussi sur leur propre capacité à s'en saisir. C'est cette observation, formulée par plusieurs partenaires du milieu, qui est à l'origine de cette recherche. Pour la première fois dans le contexte québécois, ce rapport documente, les conditions dans lesquelles les organismes à but non lucratif (OBNL) adoptent, ou non, l'intelligence artificielle générative (IAg). Il examine ces conditions à travers quatre dimensions : les caractéristiques technologiques des outils, les réalités organisationnelles internes, les pressions et ressources de l'environnement externe, et le rôle central des individus dans le processus d'adoption. title: Quantum Entanglement Time Domain (QETD)
abstract: Quantum Entanglement Time Domain (QETD) is a novel theoretical framework proposing the creation of a "Time Domain Quantum Entanglement" (TDQED) – a computational system predicated on the instantaneous transfer of information via quantum entanglement. This system seeks to revolutionize computation by enabling simultaneous processing and parallel execution, fundamentally shifting the paradigm from classical sequential processing to a dynamic, entangled computational landscape. The core claim of this research is to establish a TDQED capable of achieving instantaneous communication and parallel computation, offering a potential breakthrough in computational capabilities. This paper details the proposed TDQED model, its underlying mechanisms, and the potential implications for future quantum computing architectures.

title: Quantum Entanglement's Non-Linear Geometric Mapping
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a profound challenge to classical intuition. This research explores the potential of utilizing non-linear geometric mappings to represent and model quantum entanglement, aiming to provide a fundamentally new framework for describing quantum state evolution and computation. We propose a novel approach that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to construct a geometric model capable of capturing the essence of this quantum phenomenon. This paper outlines the core concept, mechanisms, and potential implications of this approach, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations of traditional quantum computing models. The research will focus on establishing a rigorous mathematical foundation and demonstrating its capabilities through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations.

title: Title: Temporal Diffusion of Mathematical Proofs
abstract: The generation of mathematical proofs remains a challenging task, often relying on meticulous manual effort and susceptible to human error. This research proposes a novel system, Temporal Diffusion, which leverages a probabilistic proof engine to automatically generate and refine mathematical proofs, enhancing the likelihood of successful proofs and mitigating errors. This system employs a temporal diffusion process, iteratively modifying and validating mathematical statements, gradually refining the proof process. The core mechanism involves introducing a probabilistic proof engine that iteratively modifies and validates mathematical statements, gradually refining the proof. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional proof generation by automating the process and promoting improved reliability. This paper details the architecture, functionalities, and evaluation of the Temporal Diffusion system, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating and refining mathematical proofs.

title: Knowledge Representation Based on Concept Graphs (BCKR)
abstract: This paper introduces the Knowledge Representation Based on Concept Graphs (BCKR) framework, a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning. BCKR leverages the power of concept graphs to capture the semantic and structural relationships inherent in knowledge domains. The framework utilizes graph algorithms – including pathfinding and similarity calculations – to facilitate knowledge understanding and utilization. The core claim of BCKR is that utilizing concept graphs offers an effective means for representing and reasoning about knowledge. This document outlines the fundamental principles, key components, and potential applications of the BCKR framework, demonstrating its capability to address challenges in knowledge management and intelligent systems. We present a detailed description of the methodology, focusing on the process of building concept graphs from existing knowledge sources and employing graph algorithms for inference and discovery. The framework's strength lies in its ability to transform complex, often unstructured, knowledge into a readily processable, graph-based representation, thereby enabling more sophisticated reasoning capabilities. ---

abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing computation and information processing. This research explores the application of quantum entanglement to geometric computation, proposing a novel computational model centered around the manipulation of entangled states. This work represents a significant step towards unlocking the full potential of quantum entanglement in geometric analysis.

title: Semantic Graph Completion via Knowledge Graph Reasoning and Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Graph completion is a fundamental problem in various domains, including social network analysis, biological data integration, and sensor network management. Traditional graph completion methods often rely on simplistic assumptions about graph structure, failing to capture the nuanced semantic relationships encoded within knowledge graphs. This paper proposes a novel approach, Semantic Graph Completion via Knowledge Graph Reasoning and Generative Adversarial Networks (SGCR-GAN), to address this limitation. Our method leverages the power of knowledge graphs to guide the graph completion process while utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to effectively model the inherent uncertainty and complexity. The generator learns to predict missing edges by integrating knowledge graph embeddings, while the discriminator enforces consistency between the generated graph and the underlying semantic structure of the knowledge graph. This synergistic combination results in a more robust and semantically-aware graph completion system. The core claim of this work is that traditional graph completion methods lack the ability to incorporate complex semantic relationships within knowledge graphs. The mechanism involves training a GAN where the generator attempts to complete a graph by predicting missing edges, guided by a knowledge graph embedding and a discriminator that penalizes inconsistencies with the graph's semantic structure. This approach represents a significant advancement over existing techniques by integrating knowledge graph reasoning with generative modeling.

title: 基于自适应拓扑的量子算法验证
abstract: Quantum algorithm verification is a crucial aspect of quantum computing, ensuring the robustness and correctness of quantum computations. Traditional verification methods often rely on static validation schemes, which struggle to adapt to the dynamic nature of quantum algorithms during execution. This paper proposes a novel quantum algorithm validation framework leveraging the concept of adaptive topology, enabling dynamic adjustment of quantum algorithm parameters to enhance verification accuracy and efficiency. We detail the core mechanism, including the design of a validation algorithm that continuously monitors and modifies quantum parameter values based on the algorithm's state. The proposed framework demonstrates improved verification precision and efficiency compared to existing approaches, offering a promising pathway toward robust and scalable quantum verification.

title: Quantum State Geometry Transformation Dynamic Adjustment
abstract: This paper investigates a novel dynamic adjustment technique for quantum state geometry, leveraging the principles of quantum state geometry transformations to simplify and optimize high-dimensional quantum states. Traditional methods struggle with the complexity of high-dimensional data, presenting a significant challenge for computation and data processing. This research introduces a method that utilizes quantum state geometry transformations to streamline high-dimensional quantum states, simultaneously enhance computational efficiency and data handling capabilities. We explore the application of geometric optimization algorithms to improve the effectiveness of this adaptation. The core aim is to provide a robust and adaptable framework for tackling complex quantum systems, ultimately boosting performance in various computational tasks.

title: Explainable Deep Generative Models
abstract: This paper explores the development of explainable deep generative models, addressing the critical limitations of current deep generative models which often operate as 'black boxes,' hindering trust and control. The core claim is to design models capable of explaining their generation processes. This is achieved through the integration of interpretable modules – specifically attention mechanisms and causal inference modules – within the generative architecture. These modules allow for a deeper understanding of the model's internal decision-making. Furthermore, visualization techniques are employed to showcase the model's internal states, facilitating human comprehension. The resulting models offer enhanced transparency, increased trust, and improved controllability compared to traditional deep generative models. The focus is on theoretical design and conceptual framework, without the need for experimental validation. The key contributions lie in the systematic approach to incorporating explainability into deep generative models and the utilization of visualization for enhanced understanding.

title: Thermodynamic Entropy Flow Calculation for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling neural networks by framing information processing as the flow of thermodynamic entropy. Rather than focusing on activation function computations, we propose a framework where the dynamics of a neural network are described by the flow of entropy. We introduce the concept of "entropy flow density" and define it based on the entropy of individual neuron states. The flow is then governed by network connection strengths and the temporal evolution of these states. This approach offers a potential pathway to understanding emergent behavior in neural networks by providing a physically grounded model. The central claim is that this entropy flow perspective can reveal the underlying mechanisms driving complex computation within neural networks. The core mechanism involves quantifying the entropy associated with neuron states and simulating its flow through the network connections. This work represents a shift from traditional activation function-based models to a thermodynamic perspective, offering a new lens through which to examine the fundamental principles governing neural computation.

title: Quantum State Collapse Theory (QSCT) for Information Processing
abstract: Quantum State Collapse Theory (QSCT) proposes a radical shift in our understanding of quantum information processing, moving beyond the limitations of classical approximations. This paper explores a novel theoretical framework for analyzing and manipulating the collapse of quantum states, driven by the integration of entanglement dynamics and decoherence. We outline a new conceptual model that provides a pathway to designing algorithms capable of precisely controlling the collapse process, ultimately leading to more efficient quantum data processing. The core claim of this work is that QSCT offers a foundation for significantly improved computational capabilities in the quantum realm.

title: 基于动态拓扑的量子信息存储
abstract: Quantum information storage represents a significant challenge in the field of quantum computing due to the fragility of quantum states and the need for robust storage protocols. This paper introduces a novel quantum information storage scheme predicated on dynamic topology, aiming to enhance the efficiency and reliability of quantum information storage. We detail the core mechanism involving the construction of a quantum state within a dynamically evolving topology, leveraging the inherent robustness and adaptability of this topology to mitigate decoherence and enhance storage fidelity. The proposed approach offers a promising alternative to traditional static approaches, potentially unlocking new possibilities in quantum information processing.

title: Formal Semantics of Probabilistic Programming Languages via Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling and reasoning about uncertainty in various domains, including artificial intelligence, robotics, and finance. However, the semantics of these languages remain largely informal and often lack the precision needed for rigorous analysis and verification. This work presents a novel approach to formally defining the semantics of PPLs using abstract interpretation. Our methodology focuses on capturing the inherent uncertainty associated with probabilistic operations and their propagation through program execution. We introduce a framework based on abstract domains and abstract interpretation techniques to derive a formal semantics, allowing for the analysis of program behavior under uncertainty. This approach provides a solid mathematical foundation for reasoning about PPLs, enabling improved debugging, verification, and automated reasoning capabilities. The key contributions lie in bridging the gap between the intuitive use of PPLs and a rigorous, mathematically sound formalization.

title: Replication package Do Human and Artificial Intelligence Avatar Presenters Persuade Differently? Source Credibility, Engagement and Purchase Intention across Five European Markets
abstract: Replication package for the study "Do Human and AI Avatar Presenters Persuade Differently? Trust and Engagement Pathways to Purchase Intention in Five EU Markets". A within-subjects experiment in which 630 consumers across five EU markets (Portugal, Spain, France, Germany, Poland) each evaluated a human presenter and a script-identical AI avatar delivering the same product demonstration, on five constructs: presenter authority, presenter authenticity, consumer trust, consumer engagement, and purchase intention. Presentation modality is the only factor that varies; script, voice profile, product, wardrobe, setting, framing and production quality are held constant. This deposit contains the anonymised item-level dataset, the SmartPLS 4 import files, the complete estimation output, the reproduction guide, and the reconciliation between the SmartPLS and Python pipelines. Full documentation is in README.md. CONTENTS Dataset• SmartPLS_MGA_Long_1260.csv — the primary dataset. Anonymised item-level data in long format: 1,260 rows (630 participants × 2 presenter conditions) and 62 columns (PID, Presenter, Country, Origin, Order, Gender, AgeGroup, and the 55 items). This single file contains all the empirical data underlying the article. SmartPLS 4 import files• SmartPLS_Stage1_Human.csv and SmartPLS_Stage1_Avatar.csv — first-order measurement, 630 rows × 55 items each• SmartPLS_Stage2_Human.csv and SmartPLS_Stage2_Avatar.csv — second-order and structural stage, 13 first-order latent-variable scores plus the 5 purchase-intention items• SmartPLS_Stage2_STACKED_MICOM.csv — stacked file for MICOM permutation testing• README_SmartPLS_Import.txt — import instructions, construct-to-item assignment, and the exact estimation settings SmartPLS 4 outputs• Algorithm, bootstrapping (5,000 subsamples, BCa) and PLSpredict (10 folds × 10 repetitions) workbooks for each condition• MICOM permutation test (5,000 permutations) across conditions Documentation• Camada3_Guia_Reproducao_SmartPLS4.docx — step-by-step reproduction guide (Portuguese)• Camada3_Reconciliacao_SmartPLS_vs_Python.xlsx — coefficient-by-coefficient reconciliation of the two pipelines• Camada3_Resultados_SmartPLS4_Registo.xlsx — log of values recorded from each run• SmartPLS_Tabelas_Artigo.docx — the results tables as published, for direct comparison• Model diagrams for the measurement and structural stages (PNG and SVG) Stimuli• youtube_urls.json — the twelve stimulus videos: direct URLs, video IDs, durations and production details NOTE ON THE PAIRED DESIGN Each participant contributes both a human and an avatar observation, so the human-versus-avatar comparison must preserve participant-level pairing. SmartPLS's native PLS-MGA should not be used for this contrast, as it treats the two conditions as independent groups. The equivalence tests (TOST), the specific indirect effects and the between-condition path differences were estimated outside SmartPLS from the long-format dataset, keyed on PID; Camada3_Reconciliacao_SmartPLS_vs_Python.xlsx documents the agreement between the two pipelines. ETHICS AND RIGHTS Participants were recruited through Prolific Academic and gave informed consent under a GDPR-compliant procedure; all were debriefed. The dataset carries no recruitment identifier, no IP address, no free-text response and no timestamp; PID is an arbitrary sequence number and age is released as a two-level band. The stimulus videos are not redistributed in this deposit and are not covered by the CC BY 4.0 licence. The human presenter's likeness and voice were cleared by written consent for use as research stimuli only. The videos remain hosted on YouTube as unlisted clips, reachable by anyone holding the direct URL without a login, and are linked from youtube_urls.json. RELATION TO OTHER DEPOSITS This deposit is unrelated to Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.20381330, which is the replication package for a separate, earlier study by the same authors (a pilot of n = 145 plus a synthetic sample of N = 500). The two datasets are distinct and must not be treated as versions of one another. title: Pray Algorithm Optimization (PAO): An Astronomically Inspired Metaheuristic Based on Solar Altitude and Islamic Prayer Times for Global Optimization and Engineering Design
abstract: Most population-based metaheuristics govern the exploration–exploitation balance with a monotonically decreasing parameter, locking the search into fine-tuning early with no principled way to recover diversity. This paper introduces Pray Algorithm Optimization (PAO), whose schedule is derived from an external physical model rather than a decay rule chosen by hand: the run is mapped to a solar day, and the instantaneous solar altitude places five operators at the canonical Islamic prayer times, producing a non-monotone profile that restores diversity at fixed, planned points. PAO is validated against 42 competing algorithms over 75 benchmark functions — the classical 23-function set and the CEC-2017, CEC-2019 and CEC-2022 suites — with 30 runs of 500 iterations, and on 22 constrained engineering design problems. It ranks first of 43 algorithms on CEC-2017 (mean rank 2.17), CEC-2019 (4.55), CEC-2022 (4.38) and the engineering suite (2.96), and second on the classical set, where widespread ties at the global optimum compress the ranking. Friedman tests reject rank equality on every collection (p < 10⁻²⁶), and Wilcoxon win rates reach 86–94 % on the modern suites. On the engineering problems, PAO recovers or improves the reference optimum on 18 of 22 designs, attains the best solution found by any algorithm on 20, and is statistically net-positive against all 42 competitors. Diversity analysis shows an adaptive balance, from 4 % exploration on unimodal landscapes to 52 % on deceptive ones, while an ablation indicates the schedule acts chiefly as a variance-reduction mechanism. PAO ranks 36–41 of 43 in speed, though its complexity stays in the same class as standard swarm methods. Source code is available from the corresponding author.

title: Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

title: Easy Language in Research and Practice: Users, Modalities and Domains
abstract: This volume brings together the proceedings of KLAARA 2025, a major international conference on Easy Language and accessible communication hosted at Riga’s University of Latvia in August 2025. It showcases research and practice from across Europe, illustrating how Easy Language supports participation, information rights, and inclusion in increasingly multilingual societies. The contributions span cultural institutions, public administration, media, education, and social services, with a strong emphasis on user-involved and co-creative approaches that view people not only as recipients but as experts in accessible communication, thereby underlining the growing importance of accessible communication in contemporary societies.

title: Governing Semantic Composition to Improve LLM Output Stability
abstract: A governed classification judgment that was correct in isolation became incorrect when a neighboring output was requested from the same model on the same evidence. Reordering and routing recovered it locally but not under the full output. Correcting the governed semantic input — making explicit which definitions were authoritative and how they related, rather than leaving it for the model to infer — removed the failure under the ordinary inference path, with no change to the model and no added inference stage. Composition is semantic: inputs and requested outputs have to be governed as one system, and a semantic defect can surface as model instability.

title: Pseudorandom Matrix (PMM) Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm, the Pseudorandom Matrix (PMM) algorithm, designed to optimize machine learning models and enhance their generalization and stability. Traditional machine learning methods often prioritize efficiency, but the PMM algorithm leverages the inherent stochasticity of a pseudo-random matrix to achieve significant improvements in these critical areas. The core mechanism centers around using a matrix-based data generation and matrix manipulation to create a robust and efficient computational framework. This paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and analysis, highlighting its potential benefits for a wide range of machine learning tasks.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits on Graph Embedding Dimensionality
abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental limits governing the dimensionality of graph embeddings from an information-theoretic perspective. We leverage information bottleneck theory to constrain the information flow during embedding, focusing on capturing the essential structural characteristics of a graph while minimizing redundancy. Our analysis demonstrates that the optimal embedding dimensionality is dictated by the trade-off between information preservation and compression, ultimately converging on a value determined by the graph's inherent structure and the desired level of information fidelity. We provide a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding and guiding the selection of embedding sizes, offering a departure from empirical heuristics and presenting a novel approach to graph embedding optimization. The key result is the derivation of an information-theoretic bound on the embedding dimensionality, offering a quantifiable measure for selecting the most effective embedding size.

title: Graph-Based Modeling and Prediction of Complex Networks
abstract: This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to the modeling and prediction of complex networks. Complex networks, characterized by intricate relationships and heterogeneous nodes, pose significant challenges for traditional network analysis techniques. GNNs, with their ability to learn from graph-structured data, offer a promising approach to address these challenges. This work proposes a novel GNN architecture designed specifically for complex network analysis, incorporating both node features and graph topology. We investigate the application of this model to node classification, link prediction, and community detection tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing complex network dynamics. The presented methodology provides a robust framework for understanding and predicting behavior within diverse complex networks, ultimately contributing to advancements in fields such as social network analysis, biological pathway modeling, and transportation system optimization.

title: Dynamic Topology Clustering Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology clustering algorithm designed to address the challenges of accurately clustering complex datasets. Traditional clustering algorithms often rely on static parameters, failing to adequately adapt to the inherent structure of the data. This work proposes a method leveraging dynamic topology, dynamically adjusting cluster centers based on data properties, resulting in improved clustering quality and efficiency. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of experiments on several datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to established methods. The core mechanism utilizes a dynamic topology adjustment strategy to achieve this adaptation.

title: 基于量子纠缠的拓扑几何的自适应计算框架
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for computation beyond classical paradigms. This paper explores the application of quantum entanglement to develop a novel self-adaptive computing framework, leveraging the inherent properties of entangled states to dynamically adjust computational parameters within complex systems. We propose a method for establishing a dynamic mapping between the computational process and the entangled state parameters, enabling efficient optimization of systems exhibiting high complexity and non-linearity. The core claim centers on the ability of this framework to overcome the limitations of traditional computational methods through the utilization of quantum entanglement's self-adaptive nature. This research investigates the potential of such a framework to facilitate the design and execution of algorithms capable of achieving performance gains in challenging scenarios.

title: Quantum Random Number Generator Probability Analysis and Optimization
abstract: Quantum random number generators (QRNGs) offer a fundamentally different approach to random number generation compared to classical methods, leveraging the inherent randomness of quantum processes. However, their practical implementation and analysis often face challenges, particularly concerning the accurate characterization of the underlying probability distribution and the optimization of generation algorithms. This paper presents a comprehensive probability analysis of QRNG output, focusing on identifying and quantifying sources of bias and uncertainty. We introduce a novel framework combining quantum information theory and statistical analysis to rigorously evaluate QRNG performance. Furthermore, we propose an optimization strategy based on adaptive sampling techniques and error correction, aiming to enhance both the security and efficiency of QRNGs. Our approach provides a detailed understanding of QRNG behavior and offers actionable insights for designing and deploying robust QRNG systems. The core of our analysis lies in the precise determination of the output probability distribution, denoted as P(s1, s2, ..., sK), where K represents the number of bits generated. We demonstrate how this distribution can be refined through iterative statistical estimation and how this information can be used to improve the generation process.

title: Algorithmic Bias Mitigation via Quantum Bias
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to address algorithmic bias in machine learning models. Current machine learning systems often exhibit systematic biases due to the data they are trained on, leading to unfair or discriminatory outcomes. We propose a novel algorithmic approach utilizing quantum entanglement to actively mitigate this bias by manipulating quantum states to counter correlated noise. The core mechanism involves the design of a quantum stabilizer that monitors and corrects correlated noise within the model, offering a fundamentally different approach than traditional bias mitigation techniques. We outline the theoretical framework, the proposed quantum algorithm, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Dynamic Program Synthesis and Optimization
abstract: This paper proposes a novel compiler architecture centered around dynamic program synthesis and optimization. The core idea is to create a compiler that autonomously generates and optimizes code based on program requirements. This is achieved by integrating program synthesis techniques with optimization methodologies. The system dynamically adapts to diverse programming needs, aiming to improve code efficiency and flexibility. The system utilizes a layered approach: a synthesis engine generates initial code solutions, followed by an optimization engine which refines these solutions based on pre-defined goals and heuristics. The key innovation lies in the compiler's ability to learn and adapt, leading to more efficient and tailored code generation compared to traditional static compilation. The paper outlines the core components, the proposed methodology, and the potential impact of this dynamic compilation approach. The overall architecture is designed for modularity and extensibility, allowing for the incorporation of new synthesis and optimization techniques.

title: Explainable AI Proof Framework
abstract: The increasing deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems across diverse domains necessitates a critical examination of their decision-making processes. Currently, many AI models, particularly deep neural networks, operate as "black boxes," making it challenging to understand *why* they arrive at specific conclusions. This paper proposes and outlines a formal Explainable AI (XAI) proof framework designed to rigorously verify the interpretability of AI model decisions. The framework leverages logical reasoning and formalized models to translate AI decision processes into formal logical expressions. These expressions are then subjected to formal verification, providing a trustworthy and demonstrable proof of interpretability. This approach offers a significant advancement over existing XAI methods, which often rely on subjective assessments or post-hoc explanations, by providing a mathematically sound and verifiable guarantee of interpretability. The core contribution lies in establishing a systematic and reliable methodology for ensuring that AI models are truly understandable, rather than simply appearing so.

title: Quantum Information Modality Adaptive Algorithm Design
abstract: Quantum Information Modality (QIM) is a rapidly evolving field with immense potential for revolutionizing various computational tasks, including optimization, machine learning, and cryptography. QIM offers a fundamentally different approach to quantum computation compared to existing algorithms, leveraging the inherent dynamic nature of quantum states. This paper investigates the design of a novel QIM algorithm that employs adaptive modulation techniques to enhance algorithm efficiency and accuracy. We propose a dynamic modulation scheme based on a feedback loop, where the algorithm dynamically adjusts the quantum state to optimally address the input data. The core mechanism centers around the concept of "dynamic modulation," which allows the algorithm to adapt its state based on the input's characteristics, thereby enhancing its performance. This paper details the algorithm's architecture, explores its theoretical underpinnings, and presents preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness. The benefits of this adaptive approach are highlighted, offering a significant advancement in the design of QIM algorithms.

title: Qubits of a Feather, Flawed Together: A Comparative Analysis Review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared in the context of Physics. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of quantum computing and qubits as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Physics.

title: Core Claim: Design a self-adaptive algorithm based on quantum entanglement, capable of dynamically adjusting algorithm parameters in response to small changes in input data, thereby enhancing algorithm adaptability.
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers a potentially transformative approach to algorithm design. This research investigates the implementation of a self-adaptive algorithm leveraging quantum entanglement to enhance algorithmic adaptability. The core concept revolves around utilizing entangled states to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters in response to subtle variations introduced by input data. This approach contrasts with traditional algorithms that utilize fixed parameters, potentially addressing limitations in handling complex and dynamic environments. The study details the design and implementation of this novel algorithm, providing a framework for adaptive algorithm optimization based on quantum entanglement principles. The research explores the potential advantages and challenges associated with this methodology, focusing on its capacity to maintain performance under varying input conditions and demonstrate a significant improvement in algorithm robustness compared to static parameter-based approaches. The core mechanism utilizes quantum entanglement to establish a dynamic relationship between input data and algorithm parameters, fostering a self-correcting and adaptable system. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of this approach, outlining the theoretical foundation, implementation details, and preliminary experimental results supporting its efficacy. The investigation will assess the algorithm's sensitivity to input fluctuations, its ability to maintain accuracy across a range of data variations, and its overall performance in a simulated environment. evidence.abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers a potentially transformative approach to algorithm design. This research investigates the implementation of a self-adaptive algorithm leveraging quantum entanglement to enhance algorithmic adaptability. The core concept revolves around utilizing entangled states to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters in response to subtle variations introduced by input data. This approach contrasts with traditional algorithms that utilize fixed parameters, potentially addressing limitations in handling complex and dynamic environments. The study details the design and implementation of this novel algorithm, providing a framework for adaptive algorithm optimization based on quantum entanglement principles. The research explores the potential advantages and challenges associated with this methodology, focusing on its capacity to maintain performance under varying input conditions and demonstrate a significant improvement in algorithm robustness compared to static parameter-based approaches. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of this approach, outlining the theoretical foundation, implementation details, and preliminary experimental results supporting its efficacy. The investigation will assess the algorithm's sensitivity to input fluctuations, its ability to maintain accuracy across a range of data variations, and its overall performance in a simulated environment. The ultimate goal is to establish a robust and adaptable algorithm design strategy leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement.

title: 基于量子拓扑的非局域计算框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for non-local quantum computation based on quantum topology. Traditional quantum computation often restricts itself to local, gate-based operations, limiting its potential for complex, non-intuitive algorithms. We propose a quantum topology-driven framework that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement and topology to enable algorithms with enhanced expressive power and adaptability. This framework offers a fundamentally different approach to quantum computation, potentially unlocking new possibilities for complex problem-solving and exploring applications beyond the scope of standard quantum algorithms. The core mechanisms involve the creation of topological quantum circuits, utilizing entanglement to perform operations that are inherently non-local, and the design of algorithms that exploit these topological properties for enhanced computational capabilities. This work investigates the potential of this framework to expand the landscape of quantum computation and explores its applicability to various non-local tasks.

title: Title: Dynamical Complexity Metric (DCM) for Data Analysis
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamical Complexity Metric (DCM), a novel metric designed to quantify the complexity of data structures and algorithms. Traditional complexity measures often fall short, failing to adequately capture the dynamic interplay of factors influencing performance. The DCM leverages a dynamically adaptive approach, integrating statistical properties and structural characteristics to provide a more accurate and robust assessment of computational cost. The core mechanism centers around a novel weighting function that adjusts based on the data distribution, optimizing for computational efficiency. This revised approach addresses limitations of existing metrics by offering a deeper understanding of data complexity, potentially leading to more efficient algorithm design and optimization. The research explores the practical implications of the DCM, demonstrating its effectiveness through illustrative examples and a preliminary analysis of its predictive capabilities.

title: Modelometry: Classification of Flagship AI Model Families Based on Inter-Model Stylometry
abstract: Working paper and open data. Studies that measure the output of more than one AI language model consistently find that the models write differently, in the same manner that human authors have different writing styles. We coin the term **modelometry** for the measurement and attribution of the inter-model writing style of AI systems, and **modelolect** for the style itself, formed on the pattern of idiolect and sociolect. The study asks whether the modelolect of a flagship model family is strong enough for a classifier that reads only surface stylometric features to classify the AI family that originally wrote a text. We test seven families (GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, Llama and Qwen) against human text, in two registers (formal academic text, and informal chat text) and with three tiers of features. Every AI text used is from corpora generated for our prior studies or from open datasets. On academic text, a gradient boosting classifier over 47 interpretable stylometric features attributes 7 classes (human and six families) at 73.7% accuracy against a 14.3% chance rate, and 6 classes on a second corpus at 79.2%. On chat responses from the LMArena preference dataset, the same 47 features attribute all seven families at 63.9%, and a character n-gram model with model names masked reaches 87.0%, so the small interpretable feature set accounts for about three quarters of the attributable signal. The confusion structure is also informative, since DeepSeek is rarely confused with GPT (3% in the corpus where DeepSeek is most identifiable), so the writing-style evidence does not support the claim that 'DeepSeek behaves as a distillation of GPT'. The largest confusion in the chat register is between Qwen and GPT, at about 16%. Claude is the most identifiable family in both registers. A classifier trained on academic AI generated rewrites achieves only 18.6% on chat text from the same families, so a modelolect is specific to *register*, and to *model version*, and attribution requires training data from the register it will judge. As a byproduct we release inter-family vocabulary lexicons built with the log-odds method of our study on AI vocabulary. As a final experiment, after one TextPulse humanization, *p(human)* under the family classifier increases for 87 to 98% of the texts, a majority of the humanized texts classify as human, and the source family is recovered for at most 3% of them. All features, statistics, scores and code are made publicly available for future work. Files: the paper (PDF), per-text feature tables and classifier scores for every experiment, the confusion matrices and results, the per-family vocabulary lexicons, and the scripts and figures. Raw texts from the LMArena and HAP-E datasets are not redistributed; the released sampling code (fixed seed) reconstructs the exact samples from the public datasets.

title: Declaratively Populating Wikibases with WBML
abstract: Purpose: This paper addresses the lack of a general declarative approach for generating Wikibase content from heterogeneous data sources. Existing declarative mapping approaches mainly target Resource Description Framework (RDF), while Wikibase-oriented solutions are often limited in scope or procedural in nature. We therefore propose the Wikibase Mapping Language (WBML), a declarative mapping language tailored to the Wikibase statement model. Methodology: WBML was designed by reusing selected RML concepts for logical sources and iterations, while introducing Wikibase-specific constructs. We implemented a Python prototype that translates WBML into intermediate RDF Mapping Language (RML) and RDF representations, executes them with Morph-KGC, and ingests the results into Wikibase. Findings: The study shows that declaratively generating Wikibase statements from heterogeneous sources is feasible. We also reported on a demonstration using complex JSON and a simpler, real-world use case for our institution, using CSV files. WBML supports the generation of entities, fingerprints, statements, qualifiers, references, and ranks. Value: This work provides a basis for declarative construction of Wikibase knowledge graphs from heterogeneous sources. It demonstrates how established ideas from the RDF mapping community can be adapted to other types of knowledge graphs. Future work includes supporting newer RML features not yet supported by reused components and managing updates.

title: AI Contextual Measurement for Recovering Individual and Group-Level Effects: Validation Against Survey Measures and an Occupational Application
abstract: Researchers increasingly use artificial intelligence to construct measures of social, organizational, and occupational characteristics that are absent from conventional surveys. We propose AICOME, AI COntextual MEasurement, a framework for evaluating whether AI-derived respondent-level measures can recover individual and group-level effects in contextual models. The key idea is that an AI measure constructed at the respondent level can be used to derive its group-level aggregate and its individual deviation, allowing researchers to estimate both between-group and within-group associations rather than treating AI measurement as response prediction alone. We validate the framework using the 2022 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), where occupations provide the empirical grouping structure and several job-related survey variables provide validation benchmarks. For computer use, foreign-language use, weekly hours, and management responsibilities, we compare survey measures with AI-derived measures in response-level, model-level, contextual, and boundary-condition validations. The results show that AI contextual measurement can recover much of the contextual-model information contained in observed survey variables when rich respondent and job characteristics are available. Weekly hours provides the strongest validation case, with AI-derived measures reproducing the large negative between- and within-occupation associations with satisfaction observed in CFPS. The framework also identifies clear boundary conditions: performance deteriorates when information is restricted to occupation and basic demographics, and recovery is weaker when several related concepts are treated as simultaneously unobserved. The findings suggest that AICOME is most useful for recovering a limited number of theoretically important constructs from rich existing datasets.

title: The Shape of Ownership: Verifying LLM Provenance through Semantic Structures
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly redistributed, adapted, and served behind opaque APIs, model ownership can no longer be established reliably by inspecting model internals or deployment records. This creates a need for behavioral signatures that remain observable through black-box interaction. Yet most existing black-box fingerprints instantiate ownership signals through fixed query-key associations, reducing model identity to sparse memorized associations detached from ordinary behavior and limiting both robustness and stealth (e.g., fine-tuning or quantization) and stealthiness. A stronger fingerprint should instead be distributed, naturally elicited, and expressed at a higher semantic level. To this end, we introduce PROSE (Provenance through Relational Organization of Semantic Expression), replacing fixed query sets with a target semantical domain and brittle response keys with semantic structures internalized as domain-conditioned response behavior. Specifically, the fingerprint is encoded in how the model semantically organizes its in-domain conclusions, rather than in particular tokens or prescribed outputs. PROSE constructs a private bank of domain-specific semantic templates, internalizes them through mixed fine-tuning on structurally verified and clean responses, and verifies ownership by detecting the designated structures in responses to held-out natural queries. Extensive experiments across multiple model architectures, scales, and target domains show that PROSE achieves a 100% fingerprint detection rate on unmodified models with no observed false positives, preserves model utility, and retains strong detectability under downstream modifications and output transformations.

title: Accumulated-Variance Functionals of Hidden Markov and Semi-Markov Processes: Finite-Sample Upper and Lower Bounds
abstract: We study two accumulated variance functionals for stationary two-state hidden Markov or hidden semi-Markov process, observed through a single trajectory, and separate identifying these observable quantities from recovering the latent parameters behind them. For bounded durations, inverting block moments gives finite-sample upper bounds, worked out with fully explicit constants for a capped-geometric Gaussian family; on fixed interior classes, the corresponding two-point lower bounds have the same rate. On prescribed local persistence cells a long-lag estimator matches the regular and saturated regimes-though only cell by cell, with a lag built around the cell's own scale, not through any single estimator that adapts across unknown scales. Unbounded durations known only through two moments are a separate matter: no uniform exponential bound is claimed there either.

title: AI-Powered Chatbots and the Enhancement of Customer Service and Personalization in Corporate Supermarkets: Evidence from Bayelsa State, Nigeria
abstract: This study examines the effect of AI-powered chatbots on customer service quality and personalization in corporate supermarkets in Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Three dimensions of AI powered chatbot functionality conversational intelligence, 24/7 service availability, and personalization capability are tested against two dependent outcomes: customer service quality and customer personalization experience. Using primary data collected from 238 retail customers across five corporate supermarkets in Yenagoa through a structured questionnaire, the study employs simple regression analysis to test three null hypotheses. Results show that conversational intelligence (β = 0.511, R² = 0.261, p < 0.01), 24/7 service availability (β = 0.474, R² = 0.225, p < 0.01), and personalization capability (β = 0.493, R² = 0.243, p < 0.01) each significantly predict customer service and personalization outcomes. These findings establish that AI chatbot adoption is not merely a technological novelty but a commercially consequential capability that tangibly improves the customer experience in Nigeria's growing organized retail sector. Practical and policy implications for retail managers, technology providers, and consumer protection regulators are discussed.

title: 基于动态概率的图神经网络
abstract: The present study explores a novel graph neural network architecture, termed Dynamic Probability Graph Neural Network (DPGNN), designed to enhance prediction accuracy through real-time topology adaptation. Traditional graph neural networks often struggle with evolving data distributions, necessitating a static topology. DPGNN leverages a dynamic probability approach to dynamically adjust the graph's topology, enabling it to adapt to changing data patterns. We present a methodology demonstrating significant improvements in prediction performance across a range of benchmark datasets. This work offers a promising approach to address the limitations of static graph neural networks, particularly in dynamic and complex scenarios.

title: Quantum State Collapse Prediction via Entanglement-Based Dynamics
abstract: Quantum state collapse is a fundamental challenge in quantum computing, representing a significant hurdle in achieving reliable computation. This research explores a novel method for predicting collapse based on entanglement dynamics, aiming to significantly improve error mitigation techniques. We propose a dynamic model that visualizes the evolution of entanglement as the system approaches collapse, allowing for more precise forecasting of quantum states. This approach leverages the inherent correlations within entangled systems, providing a pathway toward enhanced error correction and improved quantum algorithm performance. The method offers a distinct and potentially transformative perspective on this critical problem.

title: The Advancement of Data Analysis and Modeling Through the Integration of High-Dimensional Data Structures and Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the integration of high-dimensional data structures and graph neural networks to enhance data analysis and modeling capabilities. The core challenge lies in leveraging the strengths of both paradigms – the inherent connectivity of graphs and the ability of neural networks to learn complex patterns – to achieve significant improvements in efficiency and the discovery of underlying structural and relational insights within high-dimensional datasets. We present a novel framework that combines these elements, utilizing graph neural networks to accelerate analysis and modeling and automatically identify patterns. The paper details the design of the integration strategy, explores the benefits of this fusion approach, and discusses potential applications across various domains.

title: 自适应拓扑的非局域性量子算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm based on adaptive topology, leveraging the non-locality of quantum entanglement to achieve dynamic modeling of quantum states and enhanced physical simulation and numerical computation. Traditional quantum algorithms often require manual parameter tuning, hindering efficiency. Our proposed algorithm utilizes a dynamically constructed topological structure to represent and manipulate quantum states, offering automated optimization and improved performance. We explore the application of this approach to specific quantum simulations, demonstrating its potential to overcome limitations of existing methods. The core mechanism involves the construction of a complex topology, which facilitates the exploration of complex quantum states and facilitates efficient computation. This work contributes to the field of quantum algorithms by introducing a new approach that explicitly utilizes non-locality for dynamic modeling.

title: Recursive Self-Organizing Information Matrix
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to information matrix construction utilizing a recursive self-organizing algorithm. Traditional matrix calculations often require manual design and lack the ability to adapt to evolving data. Our work proposes a fundamentally different algorithmic framework, leveraging self-organization to dynamically adjust matrix structure, enabling automated information extraction and analysis. The core mechanism focuses on a hierarchical structure with iterative refinement, optimized for adaptability and efficient processing of dynamic datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its capacity to handle complex data patterns and achieve significant performance gains compared to conventional methods. The resulting matrix provides a robust and automated foundation for various information processing tasks.

Traditional GNN algorithms often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to effectively handle dynamic network structures. This work introduces an AGNN algorithm that dynamically adjusts the network's parameters to optimize performance in complex graph environments. We propose a novel self-adaptation mechanism centered around a gradient-based weighting scheme for node and edge features, allowing the network to adapt to the specific characteristics of the graph. The implementation demonstrates improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing GNN methods on benchmark datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of this adaptive approach.

title: Quantum-Inspired Data Augmentation for Computer Vision
abstract: This paper proposes a novel data augmentation technique inspired by quantum mechanics, specifically leveraging the principles of superposition and quantum random access memory (QRAM) simulation. Traditional data augmentation methods often rely on simple transformations like rotations, flips, and color jittering, which may not fully capture the inherent variability within a dataset. Our approach aims to generate more diverse and realistic augmented data by simulating a QRAM, effectively creating multiple correlated versions of training images simultaneously. The core idea is to represent each training image as a superposition of multiple states, allowing us to explore a vastly larger solution space than conventional methods. We quantify the augmentation process using metrics related to image entropy and feature space coverage. Preliminary simulations indicate that this quantum-inspired augmentation can significantly improve the robustness and generalization performance of computer vision models compared to standard augmentation techniques. Further research is planned to explore the practical implementation of this concept and its scalability.

title: Neuromorphic Reservoir Computing with Adaptive Reservoir Shaping via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reservoir computing (RC) is a promising approach to nonlinear time-series prediction and processing, offering a computationally efficient alternative to traditional recurrent neural networks. However, the performance of RC systems is highly dependent on the careful tuning of the reservoir's parameters – specifically, the eigenvalue distribution and synaptic connectivity. Manually adjusting these parameters is a tedious and often suboptimal process. This paper proposes a novel framework for adaptive reservoir shaping in RC systems utilizing reinforcement learning (RL). The RL agent learns to dynamically modify the reservoir parameters in real-time, responding to the input signal and optimizing the system's performance. The core claim is that RC performance is sensitive to reservoir parameters, and the proposed method leverages RL to address this sensitivity. The system is defined as: (xt, s1, s2, ..., sK), where xt is the input signal at time t, and (s1, s2, ..., sK) represents the reservoir parameters. The RL agent's policy, π(s), determines the changes to the reservoir parameters. The objective function to be minimized is the prediction error: E(t) = ||yt - h(xt, st)||2, where yt is the output, h(xt, st) is the reservoir output, and st represents the reservoir parameters at time t. The RL algorithm is based on the Q-learning method, updating the Q-values based on the reward signal. The reward signal is designed to reflect the reduction in prediction error. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, showing improved performance compared to traditional RC systems with fixed parameters. Key aspects explored include the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the RL agent's policy and the stability of the adaptive reservoir shaping process. The core mechanism involves a continuous feedback loop between the input signal and the reservoir parameter adjustments. The system's performance is evaluated using metrics such as Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).

title: Adversarial Robustness Certification for Federated Learning via Randomized Smoothing
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising paradigm for training machine learning models across decentralized devices while preserving data privacy. However, recent research has demonstrated that FL systems are susceptible to adversarial attacks, where maliciously crafted inputs can significantly degrade model performance. This paper addresses the critical issue of adversarial robustness in FL by proposing a novel approach combining randomized smoothing and formal verification. We leverage randomized smoothing to generate robust models and then utilize formal verification techniques to provide certified robustness guarantees against adversarial perturbations. Our method ensures that the trained FL model will maintain a certain level of accuracy even when subjected to adversarial attacks within a specified bounded range. The key contribution lies in the synergistic integration of these two approaches, offering a practical and theoretically sound solution for building secure and reliable FL systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a detailed analysis and theoretical framework, establishing a foundation for future research in this area.

title: Cognitive Computing Architectures Based on Temporal Logic and Event Processing
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive computing architecture that leverages the strengths of temporal logic and event processing. The core claim is that temporal logic provides a rigorous framework for specifying and verifying the desired behavior of cognitive systems, while event processing enables the system to dynamically adapt and respond to changing circumstances in real-time. The developed architecture is a hybrid system integrating temporal logic reasoning with event-driven processing, allowing for both precise specification and adaptive behavior. The key innovation lies in the synergistic combination of formal verification techniques with real-time responsiveness, a critical element often missing in current cognitive system designs. This architecture offers a pathway towards creating more reliable and robust cognitive systems by explicitly capturing and enforcing temporal constraints while maintaining the ability to react effectively to unforeseen events. The architecture is described in detail, outlining the components and their interactions, and highlighting the advantages of this combined approach.
